title: India's Pay Raises Are Widening the Gap Between Formal and Informal Workers
excerpt: Informal wages rose just 3.88% to ₹1,46,550 a year in 2024-25 while formal pay grew 9.2%, leaving 88% of informal workers below the ₹17,498 monthly benchmark, ASUSE and PLFS data show.
body:
• India's informal workers earned an average of ₹1,46,550 in 2024-25, up just 3.88% in a year, while regular salaried employees averaged ₹20,435 a month, official survey data show.
  • Nearly 88% of informal-sector workers take home less than ₹17,498 a month — the Delhi minimum-wage benchmark cited in the analysis — and only about 12% earn above it.
  • The gender gap persists inside every category: urban women in salaried jobs earn ₹26,218 a month against ₹28,776 for men, and rural casual women earn ₹304 a day against ₹425 for men.
  • The statutory wage floor of ₹178 a day is widely ignored, keeping most of India's workforce outside the gains of headline economic growth.

Wage growth in India is splitting the workforce in two. Workers in the informal economy — the overwhelming majority of the country's labour force — saw average annual earnings rise just 3.88% to ₹1,46,550 in 2024-25, while employees in regular salaried jobs averaged ₹20,435 a month, according to an India Today analysis of the latest Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) and Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) data. The raises are real, but they are landing unevenly — and for most workers, barely at all.

Two Indias in the Pay Data

The ASUSE figures put the average informal worker's annual emolument at ₹1,46,550, up from ₹1,41,071 the year before. Set against the benchmarks used in the analysis, the level is stark: nearly 88% of informal-sector workers earn less than ₹17,498 a month, and only about 12% cross that threshold. Wage growth in the informal sector has slowed to 3.9%, less than half the 13% recorded previously, even as formal-sector wages grew 9.2% and overall GDP growth is expected at 7.5% to 7.8% for fiscal 2025-26, according to survey reporting on the PLFS and ASUSE releases. Job creation in the informal economy also slowed, adding 74.5 lakh positions in 2025 against 1.1 crore earlier.

The Gender Gap Inside Every Category

The divide runs along gender lines in every segment the surveys measure. In urban salaried jobs, women earn ₹26,218 a month against ₹28,776 for men; in rural salaried jobs the gap is wider, at ₹15,898 against ₹20,401. Casual work shows the sharpest split: rural women earn ₹304 a day against ₹425 for men, and urban women ₹405 against ₹598. Women's salaried earnings did grow faster — 7.2% against 5.8% for men — and their share of salaried roles rose to 18.2% from 16.6% in 2024, but women still earn 76% of men's income in salaried work, just 36% in self-employment and 69% in casual labour.

A Floor That Is Widely Ignored

Part of the problem is enforcement. The legal wage floor of ₹178 a day, or ₹4,628 a month, is widely ignored, and most employment in India remains informal or weakly protected, leaving workers without the bargaining power or social security that formal contracts carry. One reform in motion would widen the formal safety net: a proposal to raise the Employees' Provident Fund wage ceiling from ₹15,000 to ₹30,000 a month would pull millions more workers into provident fund and pension coverage — but only those already in formal employment.

What It Means

For households, the arithmetic is direct: a 3.88% nominal raise against food, rent and transport inflation leaves most informal workers standing still or slipping back, even in a year of strong headline growth. For policymakers, the surveys make the same point from two directions — the formal economy is generating the wage gains, and the informal economy, where most Indians actually work, is not. Closing that gap, through floor-wage enforcement, wider social security coverage and movement of workers into regular salaried jobs, is the test the next round of labour data will measure.
